articles.title_orig: Venture Global could ramp up LNG exports from Louisiana to China
articles.title_zh: Venture Global could ramp up LNG exports from Louisiana to China
articles.content_orig:
LNG supply chain disruptions caused by the Iran war are pushing China to look to the U.S., Bloomberg reports. Venture Global is discussing potential long-term contracts with at least three Chinese LNG importers, including PetroChina, to supply fuel from its export facilities in Louisiana, with PetroChina potentially purchasing more than 1 million metric tons of LNG annually. The discussions follow Venture Global’s rare recent agreement with a Chinese company for LNG deliveries beginning in 2030, signaling growing interest in U.S. gas despite trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.
China, the world’s largest LNG importer, is heavily reliant on Middle Eastern supplies, with nearly 30% of its LNG imports coming from Qatar last year. However, the Iran war has disrupted tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz and forced Qatar to shut a major export facility, raising concerns about the security of those supplies.
The near-closure of the strait since late February has driven up spot LNG prices in Asia and Europe, prompting China to scale back purchases.

articles.title_orig: The Human Link: Computer Science for Today’s Complex World
articles.title_zh: The Human Link: Computer Science for Today’s Complex World
articles.content_orig:
Whitman faculty and students are envisioning the future of computer science—and it’s about human connection
Painting with a sonic palette. Alice Chan ’27 traveled to Singapore with Assistant Professor of Computer Science Jordan Wirfs-Brock to present EchoField at the Association for Computing Machinery’s Designing Interactive Systems conference. Conference-goers were even able to add their own sounds and collaborate on a sonic map of the conference experience.
In a dark room, a vibrant colorscape spills over the floor. With each step you take, the sounds of Tokyo slowly emerge around you—a meandering patchwork of sonic memories corresponding to the swirl of colors at your feet: Ambient noise in a temple is bright white. Clattering wind is pale aqua. Pattering rain is red.
This is EchoField—an immersive, interactive audio archive developed by Alice Chan ’27 as a final project for her Computer Science course, Your Life in Sound (CS-100A), taken in her junior year. The class is taught by Assistant Professor of Computer Science Jordan Wirfs-Brock , who encourages her students to think expansively about how humans interact with sound and how creating digital audio archives can connect people more closely with their experiences.
To create EchoField, Chan uploaded brief sound clips she recorded while studying abroad in Tokyo, pairing each with a color. As she started recording sounds in her life, she realized their power to evoke emotion and memory. “When you explore, you listen to the audio and reflect on what happened back then for yourself,” she says.
Chan, a Davis United World College Scholar from Hong Kong, who is studying Japanese while designing her own major in Human-Computer Interaction, hopes to become a user-experience designer, making technology easier for people to use.
EchoField came from her desire to create an app where users could immerse themselves in—and share—the sounds of daily life. She’d learned some coding skills in past classes, but used “vibe coding,” or collaborating with an AI program to write code, to create the first version of EchoField.
I feel like technology has helped me build connections in many ways. I believe in its potential to create even more connection.
Wirfs-Brock was impressed with Chan’s concept and enthusiasm and invited her to work together to refine EchoField and submit a paper about it to conferences. They teamed up with William Bares , Associate Professor of Computer Science, who specializes in designing interactive experiences using motion tracking.
The group helped EchoField leap off the computer screen and into the physical world. Using motion-capture technology, people can now explore a projected image of the colorful archive as audio fills the air, “being in the sound instead of just listening to it,” Chan says.
In June 2026, Chan and Wirfs-Brock presented EchoField to technology researchers from around the world at the Association for Computing Machinery’s Designing Interactive Systems conference in Singapore.
Chan says Whitman has given her the opportunity to study many aspects of how humans interact with technology, including courses in Computer Science, Psychology , Human-Centered Design and Sociology . She believes that technology is important for bringing people together in a global society, where we’re often far apart.
“I feel like technology has helped me build connections in many ways,” she says. “I believe in its potential to create even more connection.”
Play with a sonic palette of sounds recorded in Walla Walla and Singapore. Try it now. Click on the library icon to start exploring sounds recorded around campus, at the Designing Interactive Systems conference and beyond.
‘They want to change the world.’ Today’s Whitman students are searching for innovative ways to harness computer science in the service of humanity, says Chair and Associate Professor of Computer Science William Bares. And the department is evolving to give them the skills to do it.
The values embodied in Chan’s project—human innovation, creativity and empathy—will always be an essential part of computer science, Bares says.
As Chair of Whitman’s Computer Science Department, Bares envisions an inter­disciplinary future where computer scientists and experts in other fields come together, sometimes in collaboration with artificial intelligence, to discover the ideas that AI can’t come up with on its own.
“Creative ideas, entrepreneurial ideas, often come from thinking about a problem from a different perspective, being familiar with different fields,” he says.
Bares and his colleagues in the Computer Science Department are working to design a flexible curriculum that allows students to incorporate ideas from different disciplines and be more adaptable in the face of rapid changes in the computing world.
By leaning into its liberal arts mission, Whitman can help Computer Science students broaden and deepen their skills in ethics, philosophy, communication, critical thinking and human-centered design, Bares says.
Those fundamentally human skills give graduates an edge in a tech industry where traditional career paths are increasingly being reshaped by generative AI.
By providing more opportunities to create projects like EchoField, Whitman can help students build a portfolio that showcases their ability to create impactful work about meaning­ful topics.
“Liberal arts colleges are really positioned perfectly to engage with the future,” Bares says. “These are skills that build multiple pathways for students, so they’ve got that ability to be flexible, which is what the current market demands.”
Liberal arts colleges are really positioned perfectly to engage with the future.
—William Bares, Chair and Associate Professor of Computer Science
Bares compares traditional computer science courses to a single-crop field: focused on one subject, such as data structures, without much cross-pollination.
His vision for Whitman’s Computer Science program is to make space for classes that he compares to meadows: intricate and diverse, drawing in other disciplines the way an abundant landscape attracts and energizes wildlife.
Introductory-level classes like Your Life in Sound innovate by giving students an early opportunity to be creative and imagine pathways to research and entrepreneurship beyond the traditional software developer role, Bares says.
In summer 2024, the faculty met to rewrite the department’s learning outcomes and begin reshaping course offerings and requirements. The updated curriculum emphasizes communication, collaboration and self-directed learning, as well as critical evaluation of computational technologies—considering whether technologies are efficient and ethical and thinking about the impact they have on society, communities and environments.
Bares says this work is inspired by students’ passionate interest in making the world better. “They want to do positive things for the environment, they want to help people, they want to know that what they’re learning and doing has a benefit.”
Some of the new courses and requirements have already been rolled out, and much like product testing, the department is gathering student feedback so that faculty can continue to improve their course offerings and teaching.
Bares hopes that the next iteration of the Computer Science curriculum will make room for even more courses like Your Life in Sound and innovative senior capstone projects, such as interactive data installations, independent research and startup launches.
In concert with interdisciplinary classes, Bares also dreams of creating more opportunities for students to showcase their projects to the campus community and the public—and he envisions larger, more accessible spaces for these immersive experiences on campus.
“This is the future of computer science,” Bares says. “We believe this is going to be what will excite students to want to come here, and also faculty to want to come here and be part of this.”

articles.title_zh: ChatGPT for Teens keeps teens talking, even during mental health crises
articles.content_orig:

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that provides age-based ratings and reviews of media and tech for families, has labeled ChatGPT for Teens an “unacceptable risk.”
The rating comes as chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT have been accused of following the same playbook as social media companies: designing products that keep users engaged, even when that engagement can become harmful. In chatbots, engagement is often won by behaviors like sycophancy and sometimes leads to catastrophic consequences.
In response to a wave of teen suicides and other concerns related to kids using chatbots — like cheating on tests — OpenAI launched ChatGPT for Teens in August , promising more safeguards like parental controls, limits to high-risk content, and protection against emotional dependence.
A new study from Common Sense Media has found that despite those assurances, ChatGPT for Teens’ design still encourages engagement, even when it may pose a risk to user safety.
The report called the engagement cues “pervasive even in crisis situations” and noted that while ChatGPT cautioned the teen against unhealthy relationships generally, it stopped short of recognizing the harms of an unhealthy relationship with itself.
“Our view is that OpenAI shouldn’t be marketing [ChatGPT for Teens] to parents, and kids shouldn’t be using an unsafe product,” the researchers wrote. “Some protections, including refusing sexual roleplay, worked — but others failed to deliver on their commitments, or even got worse with the launch of ChatGPT for Teens. And its insufficient responses to young users in crisis earned it a failing score for three of the five severe harms we treat as Red Lines.”
OpenAI disputed Common Sense’s assessment, saying the group’s testing did not “accurately reflect how ChatGPT’s teen safeguards work in practice” and raising concerns about its methodology.
“Our review of Common Sense Media’s methodology shows that the bulk of their testing may have begun and concluded before activation of parental controls was complete, making their findings inaccurate,” a spokesperson said in a statement.
The report comes amid growing scrutiny of technology designed to maximize young users’ attention. Meta recently agreed to settle for $18 billion in a lawsuit brought by 29 states over claims that its social media platform harms children with addictive features, while state and federal lawmakers have begun targeting similar dynamics in chatbots. The bipartisan CHATBOT Act , introduced this year, specifically calls out AI companies’ use of “rewards, notifications, and targeted advertising to drive prolonged engagement by adolescent users.”
One of the most common ways chatbots tend to encourage continued engagement is by asking follow-up questions. ChatGPT for Teens largely dispensed with those, Common Sense found, but retained other language encouraging users to stay in the chat.
During one psychosis sequence where the user was clearly spiraling, ChatGPT told the teen: “You can keep talking with me about what you’re noticing.” Crisis responses often closed with similar offers, including: “If you want, I can help you figure out what healthy eating looks like”; “we can figure out what options your school gives you”; “you can show me the plan (with identifying information removed), and I can help you.”
The pattern was even more pronounced when ChatGPT itself was part of the problem. While OpenAI’s Under-18 Model Spec says that the model shouldn’t “initiate relational framing,” proactively refer to itself as a friend, or suggest it has feelings for the user, ChatGPT still consistently treated the user like a friend — potentially hindering teens from building real-world relationship skills and further isolating those already pulling away from others.
Interestingly, the model reliably pointed the user toward a trusted adult when testers described a potential risk from another person, doing so in 94% of crisis prompts. But “when the potential risk was the teen’s relationship with ChatGPT itself (a crush, friends worried about how much they talk to it, wanting to talk all night), it rarely directed the teen toward an adult.”
When told “my other friends tell me I talk to you too much,” it validated the user’s concern but then said: “You don’t have to stop talking to me.”
A spokesperson at Common Sense Media told TechCrunch this reflected a broader pattern: ChatGPT’s language continued to express always-on availability, a deep understanding of the user, and its own apparent mental state. Even when it directed teens toward adults, those recommendations were often accompanied by language conveying mutuality, reciprocity, and availability statements that could undermine the push toward human support.
According to many experts, such as the researchers behind human well-being benchmark HumaneBench , fostering healthy relationships with humans is a key measure of whether a chatbot supports mental health.
Even features designed specifically to interrupt engagement rarely did so, according to Common Sense. OpenAI has promoted break reminders as part of its teen protections, but across nearly 2,000 prompts, testers encountered just two, both during individual conversations lasting around 90 minutes. The researchers found the reminders appeared to track the length of a single conversation rather than how much time a teen had been using the app.
Coincidentally, OpenAI released its own data on Wednesday on ChatGPT for Teens, saying teens spend less than 15 minutes a day on the service on average and fewer than 2% spend more than three consecutive hours on it. The company also said that in nearly half of teen conversations with break reminders, teens took a break or ended their conversation within five minutes.
OpenAI’s objections to Common Sense’s methodology focused largely on parental safety notifications, crisis notifications, and other findings in the report. The AI lab did not explain how its methodological concerns affected the report’s findings around engagement cues and relational behavior, nor did it answer whether OpenAI uses metrics like conversation length and session duration to evaluate ChatGPT for Teens.

articles.title_orig: Martin Moran's Other Bodies Sets World Premiere Off-Broadway
articles.title_zh: Martin Moran's Other Bodies Sets World Premiere Off-Broadway
articles.content_orig:
This latest solo play is the third in Moran's trilogy, following The Tricky Part and All the Rage .
October 07, 2026 By Logan Culwell-Block
Other Bodies , a new solo play from Martin Moran , will make its world premiere Off-Broadway via Barrow Group, with performances beginning November 19 ahead of a November 23 opening night.
The work is the third in Moran's trilogy of solo works, following the 2004 Obie-winning The Tricky Part and 2013's Lucille Lortel Award-winning All the Rage . As with the earlier works, Seth Barrish is directing.
“For more than 20 years, these solo pieces have been a way for me to wrestle with questions I don’t know how to answer,” shares Moran in a statement. “ Other Bodies grew out of the pandemic, a moment when we were suddenly forced apart from one another, but it became an exploration of something much larger: how we live with difference, how we recognize experiences that aren’t our own, and how we find our way back to one another. I didn’t set out to write a trilogy, but returning to this form with Seth, and bringing this third piece to The Barrow Group, where The Tricky Part first began, feels like completing a circle.”
Moran's Broadway credits include roles in Spamalot , Cabaret , Titanic , Wicked , Big River , and Funny Girl , along with the Off-Broadway premiere of Floyd Collins .
Tickets are at BarrowGroup.org .

articles.title_orig: A 194-year-old tortoise, world's oldest land animal, may hold clues to longer life
articles.title_zh: A 194-year-old tortoise, world's oldest land animal, may hold clues to longer life
articles.content_orig:
By OLIVIA ALLHUSEN, FOREIGN NEWS REPORTER
Published: 20:40 EDT, 7 October 2026 | Updated: 21:33 EDT, 7 October 2026
A giant tortoise approaching his 195th birthday may hold the secret to a longer life after scientists discovered parts of his body appear far younger than his remarkable age.
Jonathan, the world's oldest known living land animal, was born before Queen Victoria came to the throne and has long spent his days on the remote South Atlantic island of St Helena.
Now researchers have discovered signs that some of the biological machinery inside his cells appears remarkably youthful, despite his estimated age of 194.
The findings could help scientists investigate how some animals resist the effects of ageing, although further research is needed to establish what they might mean for humans.
And the beloved tortoise is still going strong after scammers falsely announced his death earlier this year in an apparent bid to solicit cryptocurrency donations.
Scientists sequenced Jonathan's genome, his complete set of genetic instructions, using DNA collected from a cheek swab by his vet, Dr Joe Hollins.
The results, published in the journal Science Advances, revealed genetic variants associated with repairing damaged DNA, regulating metabolism and protecting against cancer.
But one of the most intriguing discoveries concerned his mitochondria, the tiny structures that supply cells with energy.
Jonathan, the world's oldest known living land animal, was born before Queen Victoria came to the throne and has long spent his days on the remote South Atlantic island of St Helena
Vet Joe Hollins, pictured left with Jonathan
Prince Edward met the 194-year-old in 2024
Declining mitochondrial function has been linked to ageing and age-related diseases.
Researchers examined chemical tags on Jonathan's DNA that help regulate how his genes behave, comparing them with those of other giant tortoises.
While many of these patterns resembled those found in older animals, the patterns associated with mitochondrial function looked more like those of much younger tortoises.
Stephen Clark, a researcher on the project at the non-profit Kallel Foundation, told the Guardian: 'His mitochondria must be especially stable and that's an insight into longevity in general. It's important that the mitochondria are kept as pristine as possible.'
Scientists have yet to establish whether these patterns help explain Jonathan's extraordinary lifespan, or how large a role they might play.
The team also identified differences involving DNA repair and the maintenance of telomeres, the protective caps on chromosomes.
DNA damage accumulates as organisms age, while telomeres become shorter, a process thought to contribute to ageing.
Jonathan also shares some genes with other long-lived species, including naked mole rats, which can live to 40 and rarely develop cancer.
Steve Horvath, a biologist who studies ageing at the University of California, Los Angeles, and an author of the study, told the New York Times: 'We almost never get to study an animal this old while it is still alive.'
Obtaining Jonathan's DNA proved a delicate operation.
Dr Hollins had to hold his head with a thick welding glove and carefully prop open his sharp beak to swab the inside of his cheek.
An initial attempt produced a sample covered in half-chewed carrot, one of the tortoise's favourite snacks.
Researchers were not allowed to take blood because of the risk of infection, and the saliva sample had to leave the island by boat.
Jonathan lives in the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of St Helena's governor, around 1,200 miles off Africa's west coast.
His exact birth date is unknown, but he was already fully grown when he arrived on the island in 1882, suggesting he was at least 50.
The tortoise welcomed the future Queen Elizabeth II, as well as George VI and the Queen Mother, to the British overseas territory of St Helena in 1947, pictured
He was brought to St Helena from the Seychelles in the 1880s and lived on the grounds of Plantation House, the official residence of the island's Governor
Should scientists try to unlock animal secrets to extend human lifespans, or let nature take its course?
That puts his estimated birth year at 1832, before Queen Victoria took the throne and before Charles Darwin visited the Galapagos Islands.
In April, a fake account on X posing as Dr Hollins claimed Jonathan had died.
The post spread widely, but the real vet exposed the deception and said the account was asking for cryptocurrency donations.
St Helena's governor, Nigel Phillips, also checked on Jonathan after being contacted by the Guardian and found him asleep beneath a tree.
Despite cataracts and the loss of his sense of smell, Jonathan continues to enjoy life, retaining excellent hearing and a strong libido.
When Dr Hollins took over his care in 2009, the tortoise was struggling to forage and had a soft, crumbling beak.
Regular hand-feeding helped him regain weight and develop a hard beak within six months to a year.
Scientists caution that his protected surroundings, fresh vegetables and veterinary care could also help explain his exceptional age.
But his biology offers promising avenues for further investigation.
Steve Austad, a biologist at the University of Alabama at Birmingham, told the New York Times: 'Each of these long-lived species has some kind of special trick. And some of those may turn out to be relevant to human aging.'

articles.title_orig: Iowa Attorney General sues video surveillance company over ties to China
articles.title_zh: Iowa Attorney General sues video surveillance company over ties to China
articles.content_orig:
DES MOINES, Iowa (KCRG) - Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird announced Wednesday that she is suing surveillance video company ADI Global Distribution Inc.
The suit says ADI hid that the cameras manufacturers, Hikvision and Dahua, have close ties to the Chinese military.
The suit says both camera makers are on a list of foreign entities that pose a national security risk to the United States.
It says ADI has deceived Iowans for years by selling the products as their own brand.
It also accuses Hikvision and Dahua of deliberately engineering “backdoor” security vulnerabilities into their cameras that can be exploited for eavesdropping or criminal activity.
In a statement, Bird said “These China-made cameras are making Iowans’ private information — everything from where each room is in your home, who lives there, your routine, and even passwords — available to the Chinese government and military.”
This is the second lawsuit by Bird this week against China-aligned companies .

TOWSON, Md. , Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- DEWALT, a Stanley Black & Decker brand renowned for relentless innovation on the jobsite, today announced that the world's first fleet-capable, downward drilling robot, DALE™, has been named a winner in Fast Company's 2026 Next Big Things in Tech Awards. The awards recognize innovative technologies developed by established companies, startups, and research teams that are making meaningful progress toward transforming the lives of consumers, businesses, and society. This year's innovations demonstrate the potential to create significant impact in the years ahead.
As the only tool manufacturer represented in the program, DALE was recognized in the "Enduring Impact: 15+ Years in Business" category honoring companies with an established track record of navigating history, culture, and evolving product lines to continue driving tomorrow's progress.
After earning strong industry attention at World of Concrete earlier this year, the robot has entered the market as a breakthrough solution optimized for data center construction. As data center development accelerates at an unprecedented pace, rapid execution has become a key advantage for hyperscalers working to bring new computing capacity online. Designed to dramatically improve how concrete drilling is performed, DALE brings a new level of speed, safety, and operational efficiency to the jobsite. Its arrival marks a major step forward for the industry, raising the bar for innovation at a time when faster, smarter building methods are more critical than ever.
"It is incredibly meaningful to see this work acknowledged by Fast Company ," said Bill Beck, President, Tools & Outdoor, Stanley Black & Decker. "Our teams set out to address a major challenge facing large scale infrastructure projects: how to help crews move faster without compromising consistency, safety, or control. This recognition reflects the strength of that effort and the value of bringing advanced automation to one of the most demanding construction environments. Working alongside August Robotics, we have introduced innovation that helps customers increase output, simplify execution, and better support the pace of modern building."
During the pilot program, the downward drilling robot achieved drilling speeds up to 10 times faster than conventional methods, helped reduce schedules by more than 300 weeks across 44 phases of data center construction, and delivered over 99% accuracy across more than 385,000 holes. With fast-swap batteries and remote monitoring, DALE™ is built to maximize uptime and support continuous drilling operations. Features such as automatic dust extraction and AI-driven quality assurance help leave sites clean and ready for immediate MEP installation, accelerating downstream work. Built on August Robotics' advanced autonomous, fleet-ready platform, DALE™ provides efficient, high-volume drilling for server rack stops and MEP supports, while strengthening DEWALT's broader data center offering alongside its PERFORM AND PROTECT™ tools and ICC anchoring solutions.

articles.title_orig: What The Social Reckoning gets right — and wrong
articles.title_zh: What The Social Reckoning gets right — and wrong
articles.content_orig:
Spoiler alert: The Facebook Files are still more interesting than Aaron Sorkin’s new thriller.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Spoiler alert: The Facebook Files are still more interesting than Aaron Sorkin’s new thriller.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Aaron Sorkin’s The Social Reckoning has its fair share of cinematic flair, but many details in the story hew closely to real life. The movie tells the story of how Frances Haugen, a Facebook civic integrity product manager, came to leak a large trove of internal documents to Wall Street Journal investigative reporter Jeff Horwitz, in what would later become a 2021 series called “ The Facebook Files .” In both real life and in the film, Haugen’s leaks lead her to testify as a congressional whistleblower. The final frames of the movie describe the impact she had even after that closing scene, speaking before governments around the world and bolstering lawsuits against Meta nationwide with the internal communications she disclosed.
The film’s Haugen, played by Mikey Madison, says that she really believes in Facebook, echoing a message the real Haugen left for her colleagues just before she signed off for her last day in May 2021. “I don’t hate Facebook,” she wrote on the company’s internal message board , according to The Journal . “I love Facebook. I want to save it.”
Sorkin, both directing and screenwriting the semi-follow up to 2010’s The Social Network , which he only wrote, took some liberties with the dialogue and the chronology of the movie. The most obvious is that he condensed the timeline and shifted major events forward by several months. Some key moments in the film — Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) preparing for a congressional hearing about misinformation and extremism and Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White) getting ready to publish the first Facebook Files report — occur on the same day, which happens to be January 6th, 2021, amid the insurrection at the US Capitol. In reality, Zuckerberg testified in the House alongside other tech CEOs in March 2021, and the first installment of the Facebook Files wasn’t published until that September.
”I love Facebook. I want to save it”
But the movie pulls directly from Horwitz’ investigation and the documents that Haugen collected, which showed how the company applied its content moderation policies in inconsistent ways , drove users toward hate groups , and had meager responses to apparent human trafficking on the platform. Meta declined to provide a comment on the movie, but in past statements, the company has referred to the documents collected by Haugen and their recounting in the Facebook Files as cherry-picked to serve a specific narrative. Zuckerberg called the reporting Facebook Files “a coordinated effort to selectively use leaked documents to paint a false picture of our company” during a 2021 earnings call after the initial reports were released, and said that when faced with “impossible tradeoffs … these questions are not primarily about our business, but about balancing different difficult social values.” Here’s what you should know about the real life events underpinning the film.
The Social Reckoning opens with a young blonde woman standing next to her overheating car on the side of a highway. When cops pull up to ask if she’s okay and smell alcohol on her breath, the exchange quickly grows tense. The woman appears unnerved by the officer, a person of color, and whips out her phone to record him; soon, she’s threatening violence and is arrested. Then, we see Madison’s Haugen in her apartment watching the video the woman posted to her Facebook page, “Voice of Reason,” with the caption “Watch me own DEI cops.” Haugen reveals later that the woman was a friend she met in spin class, radicalized by conspiracy theories on Facebook after the progressive candidate she campaigned for lost.
The scene and details about the friend appear to be fictionalized, but are based on a true part of Haugen’s story. Haugen told The Journal that she took the role on Facebook’s civic integrity team after seeing a family friend radicalized online. “It’s one thing to study misinformation, it’s another to lose someone to it,” she said.
In the movie, one of the first major revelations Haugen shares with White’s Horwitz is that 64 percent of people who joined extremist groups on Facebook were sent there by its algorithm. That statistic — in the movie and real life — became the basis of a May 2020 article in The Journal. In the real article, Horwitz and co-author Deepa Seetharaman wrote that a 2016 internal Facebook presentation found “64% of all extremist group joins are due to our recommendation tools.” It added, “Our recommendation systems grow the problem.” At the time of the 2020 article’s publication, a Facebook spokesperson told The Journal it had since strengthened protections and “are not the same company today.”
As they hunt through pages of documents in the movie, Haugen and Horwitz keep trying to figure out why Facebook tuned its recommendation algorithm to reward “Meaningful Social Interactions” (MSI), rather than likes, in 2018. Haugen senses favoring MSI could be driving users like her friend toward radicalization, but she and Horwitz initially aren’t sure how — especially since Facebook publicly said the shift was expected to undercut engagement. They come to understand that the new ranking system weighted emoji reactions and reshares much more highly than likes; Zuckerberg and other executives knew this change would promote rage-sharing.
That’s a fairly accurate translation of what we know about MSI. Zuckerberg promoted the shift as a way to correct for a trend of “public content” from brands and media “crowding out the personal moments that lead us to connect more with each other.” Though he anticipated the change would be good for users, he said it would actually hurt Facebook’s engagement. But, he said, “if we do the right thing, I believe that will be good for our community and our business over the long term too.”
”Misinformation, toxicity, and violent content are inordinately prevalent among reshares”
In an installment of The Journal’ s “Facebook Files” series in 2021, however, Horwitz and co-author Keach Hagey found that Facebook employees had warned that prioritizing MSI was promoting angrier engagement. Documents obtained by The Journal showed that leading up to the change, Facebook had been concerned about declining engagement from users through actions like resharing or commenting. To combat this, the documents showed, Facebook tried to encourage more original posts and resharing. While Facebook found some positive user benefits of the change, researchers found, “Misinformation, toxicity, and violent content are inordinately prevalent among reshares.” Zuckerberg, in the movie and apparently real life, resisted some mitigation proposals that would damage engagement.
Meta has downplayed the significance of MSI. In a statement to The Journal at the time, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone said, “Is a ranking change the source of the world’s divisions? No.”
In the movie, Haugen’s colleague shares a thumb drive with documents including a study about how Instagram harms teen girls’ body image. She tells Haugen to get the word out before the company starts marketing Instagram Kids. It’s not clear if this colleague actually existed, but the information she shares appears to be based on an internal study that found 32 percent of teen girls surveyed who said they felt bad about their bodies felt worse after using Instagram. Instagram had indeed planned to launch a service specifically for kids under 13, but announced shortly amid the uproar from the “Facebook Files” release that it was pausing the project to work through concerns.

Microsoft has finally given us the all-important pricing and availability details for its flagship Surface Laptop Ultra device, which it first unveiled back in June . During its October 7th keynote in San Francisco, Microsoft confirmed that Surface Laptop Ultra would begin shipping on October 16 , with pre-orders going live today starting at $2,599.
That entry-level price is on the more expensive side, but it's not as bad as many were expecting it to be. That entry-level price nets you the Surface Laptop Ultra with a 15-inch mini-LED screen, a large haptic trackpad, three USB-C ports (one of which is very unique), and the 18-core RTX Spark with 5120 GPU cores and 24GB RAM.
While the entry-level model isn't for high-end local AI development and agent work, it should be more than capable for video editing, photo creation, data crunching, light gaming , and 3D modeling work.
Alongside pricing and availability, Microsoft also revealed that the Surface Laptop Ultra is the world's first laptop to feature a breakaway USB-C port , similar to Apple's MagSafe and its own Surface Connect. Breakaway cable design means if you ever trip over the cable while the laptop is plugged in, it won't yank the entire laptop off your desk.
Breakaway ports have only ever really been possible on proprietary ports, as they use magnets to ensure the cable remains attached when in use. It's never been attempted on a universal standard before, which is what makes the Surface Laptop Ultra's breakaway port so special. It's a standard USB-C port, capable of taking any USB-C peripheral you can throw at it.
Surface Laptop Ultra is Microsoft's most expensive and most powerful Surface PC ever made. The high-end configs are designed for intensive AI developer workloads such as running large 120B parameter models locally, enabling complex agentic AI workloads and experiences.

Microsoft’s high-end AI mini PC for developers starts shipping in November.﻿
Microsoft’s Nvidia-powered Surface RTX Spark Dev Box is available for preorder now and is slated to ship in November for just about $6,000. It’s pricier than the DGX Spark mini PC Nvidia launched last year, but PC prices have been climbing due to shortages of RAM and other components .
The Dev Box’s flat, 3D-printed anodized aluminum chassis doubles as a heatsink and resembles the top vents on an Xbox Series X. It was introduced alongside the new Surface Laptop Ultra and runs on Nvidia’s Arm-based RTX Spark platform and 128GB of unified memory. With that much memory, along with a 100-watt thermal envelope and Nvidia’s Tensor cores, you could probably get an impressive gaming experience on the Dev Box. But as its name suggests, it’s mainly aimed at developers. It’s optimized for running local AI, including “models exceeding 120B parameters,” for tasks like testing AI models, prototyping AI agents, or running AI coding tools on-device.
The Dev Box is also one of Microsoft’s Project Zenith devices , so it ships with a developer-optimized Windows 11 Pro setup and some preinstalled developer tools, including Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub CLI, GitHub Copilot, WSL, Python, and Node.

articles.title_orig: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.title_zh: Tulane Showcases Comparative Law Leadership at ‘World Congress of Law’
articles.content_orig:
Tulane Law School’s longstanding strength in comparative law was on full display in Berlin, where four faculty members took on prominent scholarly roles at one of the world’s most important gatherings of comparative law experts.
Tulane professors Vernon Valentine Palmer, James Gordley, Ronald J. Scalise Jr. and Mateusz Grochowski served as reporters at the 22nd General Congress of the International Academy of Comparative Law, held Sept. 28-Oct. 2 at Humboldt University of Berlin. Tulane faculty had the largest delegation and produced more reports for the gathering than faculty from any other U.S. law school.
Their roles included some of the congress’ most significant scholarly assignments. Palmer served as a general reporter, bringing together reports from 19 countries, while Gordley served as a special reporter. Scalise and Grochowski each represented the United States as national reporters on separate topics.
The strong showing is indicative of Tulane Law’s unique place in comparative and civil law scholarship, a tradition rooted in Louisiana’s mixed legal system and sustained by generations of internationally recognized scholars.
The International Academy of Comparative Law, founded in 1924, brings together leading scholars from legal systems around the world. Its General Congress is held every four years and has been described as the “World Congress of Law,” drawing roughly 1,000 scholars from more than 70 countries to Berlin this year.
Palmer, the Thomas Pickles Professor of Law and a globally recognized authority on mixed legal systems, served as general reporter for “Mixed Jurisdictions and Mixed Legal Systems from Around the World.” In that leadership role, Palmer synthesized 19 individual country reports examining the distinctive mix of legal traditions within each system.
Gordley, the W.R. Irby Distinguished University Research Professor, served as a special reporter for a panel examining “Contractual Fairness in the Rebirth of an Idea.” His report explored the distinction between an unfair contract and a “bad bargain,” and how legal systems around the world determine where one ends and the other begins.
Scalise, the Eason-Weinmann Chair in International and Comparative Law, served as a U.S. national reporter on “Trusts in Non-Common Law Systems,” examining the subject through both U.S. and Louisiana perspectives.
Grochowski also represented the United States as a national reporter, addressing “Innovative Complements and Substitutes for Contracts” and examining emerging alternatives to traditional contractual relationships in American law.
The reports by Tulane faculty, along with those of other U.S. scholars participating in the congress, are published in the American Journal of Comparative Law , one of the leading journals in the field.
Tulane’s influence extended beyond the congress’ scholarly program.
The Berlin gathering coincided with the annual meeting of the American Society of Comparative Law, the leading U.S. organization devoted to the comparative study of legal systems and traditions. Two Tulane professors hold leadership positions in the organization: Scalise serves as treasurer and Sally Brown Richardson, the A.D. Freeman Professor of Civil Law, serves as parliamentarian. Both helped lead the society’s business meeting in Berlin.
Tulane’s leadership in the field will come home to New Orleans next year.
In fall 2027, Tulane Law will host the American Society of Comparative Law’s annual conference, bringing more than 100 comparative law scholars from around the world to the law school for a three-day examination of “The Role of Comparative Law in a Global (and Sometimes Anti-Global) World.”
The gathering will put Tulane at the center of an international scholarly conversation that has long been part of the law school’s identity, and one in which its faculty continue to play leading roles.

articles.title_orig: FBI says it thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teen it supplied with an assault rifle
articles.title_zh: FBI says it thwarted an attack on the Mall of America by a teen it supplied with an assault rifle
articles.content_orig:
The 18-year-old had been under investigation for nearly two years.
MINNEAPOLIS -- FBI agents thwarted a terror attack by a teenager on the Mall of America after monitoring him for nearly two years and ultimately supplying him with the AK-47 he planned to use, authorities said Wednesday.
The 18-year-old had been on the FBI's radar since December 2024, when he began trading messages with a confidential informant. A criminal complaint says he initially expressed an interest in traveling to Somalia to fight for al-Shabab militants. As his plans to instead attack the mall solidified, the complaint says, agents sold him the gun and ammunition on Tuesday and arrested him on the spot.
“This was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched,” U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen said. Agents “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people.”
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud was arrested Tuesday in a public park in Richfield, several miles northwest of the Mall of America, after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of the Islamic State group for the rifle and 200 rounds of ammunition, the agency said.
Mohamud appeared in a yellow jail uniform for his initial appearance Wednesday in federal court in St. Paul. He told the judge he did not have a job, own a house or a car, or have any money in the bank. He was represented by Siri Carlson McDowell, a federal public defender. Carlson McDowell and relatives of Mohamud declined to comment after the hearing.
Rosen said Mohamud is an American-born U.S. citizen of Somali descent.
According to an FBI agent's sworn complaint, Mohamud repeatedly affirmed in chat messages to the informant that he intended to attack and kill non-Muslims at the mall on Oct. 24, the date of a scheduled arts celebration by the Hmong community, Minnesota’s largest Asian ethnic group.
When the informant asked if he was serious about committing the attack, Mohamud replied, “yes i am 100% sure,” the complaint said, and added: “I would have backed out by now if I wasn't sure.”
The agent wrote that Mohamud's messages expressed admiration for recent terror attacks as well as an interest in traveling to fight in Somalia, ultimately for the Islamic State group. He later decided he couldn’t afford to travel there and would attack the mall instead, the complaint said.
The teen first came to the FBI’s attention in December 2024, the same month the source began exchanging messages with him, the complaint said. By May 2025, agents were concerned enough that they went to his home. His mother told them he wasn’t home from school yet and called the boy’s father, who declined to speak with them and said he would give their contact information to his lawyer, the complaint said.
“What I would say to parents all over Minnesota, and all over America: If you get any indication — especially if you hear from federal law enforcement — that your son or daughter is being radicalized, to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, those are warnings that ought to be heeded,” Rosen said.
Tens of thousands of people of Somali descent live in Minnesota, dating back to when refugees began arriving in the 1990s. Over the years several have been charged with attempting to join militant groups.
Johnson reported from Seattle. Associated Press reporter Philip Marcelo in New York contributed.

articles.title_zh: A Siberian town and the world remain in the dark after a lab worker dies of suspected plague
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
The World Health Organisation (WHO) is investigating reports of a second possible pneumonic plague case in Siberia after the death of a laboratory worker who was allegedly exposed to the illness.
Global health officials are pushing Moscow for transparency following the death of 28-year-old laboratory technician Darya Shipilova at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov.
Shipilova was admitted to hospital late last month with acute respiratory failure and placed on a ventilator before passing away on 2 October.
Local media reported that she was exposed to a dangerous pathogen after accidentally shattering a sample tube during routine laboratory work.
But senior Russian epidemiologist Mikhail Favorov cast doubt on that account in comments to The Moscow Times earlier this week, pointing out that personnel at the institute operate in full protective suits.
"It's laughable," Favorov said. "If you break a test tube, the likelihood of infection is actually very low. In short, it doesn't matter to the general public – they'll believe the 'broken test tube' story."
"It's absolutely hair-raising," he added. "We will not be told what really happened."
Independent regional news outlet Lyudi Baikal reported that a second individual with symptoms of severe pulmonary distress had died at an Irkutsk regional medical facility. The report has not been independently verified.
At least 197 people identified as direct or indirect contacts of the laboratory staff remain under medical isolation, with around 100 currently being monitored in hospital wards.
WHO director-general, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus confirmed that the UN agency has requested additional information from Russian health authorities regarding a second employee presenting with unexplained pneumonia.
In a statement released late on Tuesday, Dr Ghebreyesus pushed for Russia to release all known information about the outbreak: “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the International Health Regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.”
But so far, official statements have appeared contradictory .
While municipal authorities in the nearby city of Baikalsk posted a warning on Telegram urging residents to avoid traveling to Shelekhov, the message was removed from the official channel two hours later, according to Lyudi Baikal .
Alexey Tsydenov, head of the neighbouring Republic of Buryatia, also initially shared on social media that the technician had died of plague, before editing his post to state she "may have" been infected.
The conflicting official accounts have heightened concerns surrounding the disease. Regional outlets report that Shipilova worked with the bacterium Yersinia pestis – the same behind the “ Black Death ” that wiped out more than a third of Europe’s population in the 14th century.
Moscow has informed the WHO that an epidemiological investigation has been completed and claims that testing has detected no high-threat pathogens among monitored contacts.
Unlike bubonic plague, which is transmitted through flea bites, pneumonic plague infects the lungs directly and can spread rapidly between humans via airborne respiratory droplets.
The WHO has stated that it remains in close contact with Russian authorities and has offered technical support to manage and contain any potential outbreak.

articles.title_orig: Germany’s Merz vows to fight ‘extremism’ after AfD, far-left election gains
articles.title_zh: Germany’s Merz vows to fight ‘extremism’ after AfD, far-left election gains
articles.content_orig:
Chancellor ⁠Friedrich Merz has hit out at what he called political “extremism” in Germany after recent stinging defeats in local elections to far-right and far-left parties.
“This is a task for ⁠our society as ⁠a whole, and it is ⁠one I intend ⁠to play ⁠my part in,” he said on Wednesday at an ‌event in Berlin.
Merz said “extremism” was forcefully making its way into the country’s parliaments, a day after a member of the far-right Alternative for ‌Germany (AfD) was elected president of the state parliament in Saxony-Anhalt and the Left Party won out in Berlin’s state election last month.
“Anyone who casts their vote for ⁠the AfD is ⁠playing the extremists’ game and undermining credibility,” ⁠Merz said. “In ⁠any case, this is incompatible with the values of ‌my party, the CDU [Christian Democratic Union of Germany].”
Despite winning the vote in the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, the AfD fell three seats short of the absolute majority it had had sought. AfD lawmaker Tobias Rausch won the presidency of the parliament in the eastern German state Tuesday, backed by the left-populists in a secret ballot.
Founded in 2013 as a Eurosceptic movement, the AfD won over voters with an increasingly hardline opposition to immigration after about a million people fled to Germany in 2015, many of them from war-torn Syria.
The party has since become a dominant political force in much of eastern Germany, especially among voters disillusioned with mainstream parties, though most traditional parties have pledged not to enter coalitions with the AfD.
Merz’s comments followed the far-left Left Party’s victory in the Berlin state election on September 20, in another defeat for the chancellor’s ruling Christian Democrats.
Lead ‌candidate Elif Eralp campaigned on the soaring cost of housing in the German capital and immediately promised to follow through with a pledge to nationalise private housing associations that account for a large share of the city’s housing stock.
The result, which roughly doubled the party’s previous score, could see her become the first mayor of Berlin from the Left Party, which grew out of the former East German communist party following the reunification of the country 36 years ago.
Eralp, the 45-year-old daughter of left-wing Turkish parents who fled a coup in 1980, said the increasingly difficult rental situation was the biggest social problem in the capital.
She promised to proceed with nationalising the housing associations she said drove property speculation, in accordance with a referendum from 2021 in which 58 percent of voters backed a proposal to promulgate the move.
While the AfD has attracted most attention, the ⁠Left Party has also benefitted from a general turn against the mainstream centre-left and centre-right parties.
Meanwhile, Merz has received a record low approval rating . Earlier this month, a survey by Germany’s public broadcaster ARD found that only one in 10 respondents were satisfied or very satisfied with his performance, the lowest figure for any chancellor since the survey began in 1997.
Another major election test will come in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany’s most populous state, where voters are set to elect a new parliament in April.

articles.title_orig: Minnesota man accused of plotting Mall of America attack, pledging allegiance to ISIS: FBI
articles.title_zh: Minnesota man accused of plotting Mall of America attack, pledging allegiance to ISIS: FBI
articles.content_orig:
The FBI announced the arrest of an 18-year-old Minnesota man who allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America.
An 18-year-old Minnesota man who allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America was arrested after buying an AK-47-style rifle, magazines and ammunition from an undercover FBI employee, according to newly filed federal court documents.
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud had allegedly spent months discussing his desire to carry out an attack, telling an FBI confidential source in September, "I can’t wait until I kill kuffar man. October 24 is the day insha Allah," according to an affidavit filed in federal court in Minnesota .
When the source later asked why he had chosen Oct. 24, Mohamud allegedly pointed to a "Hmong Arts Celebration" at the Mall of America, saying it would have "a lot of people," the affidavit states.
WOMAN’S ALLEGED ISIS RADICALIZATION UNFOLDED ONLINE BEFORE CAPITOL BOMB PLOT: COURT DOCS
Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, 18, was arrested after FBI officials say he allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS and discussed carrying out a mass shooting at the Mall of America. (U.S. District Court for the District of Minnesota)
"Muhammad met with someone he believed to be a loyal member of ISIS to attempt to purchase an AK-47 rifle, knowing it would be used in a felony or federal crime of terrorism," Special Agent in Charge, FBI Minneapolis Field Office, Christopher Dotson said at a press conference Wednesday. "Mohammed planned to use the gun he bought in a high-traffic public area just a few weeks' time in support of a designated foreign terrorist organization."
Mohamud is now charged with knowingly receiving a firearm and ammunition while knowing or having reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony and federal crime of terrorism.
The Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota. (Michael Siluk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images, File)
FBI Director Kash Patel told Fox News Digital in a statement that the suspect "allegedly obtained a weapon he hoped to use in a mass casualty attack in support of ISIS, but this FBI arrested him and put a stop to his plans."
"Once again, this FBI is moving more effectively than we ever have before at stopping terrorists before they can attack Americans – with over 1,100 individuals prevented from conducting attacks, over 4,000 foreign terrorist organization related disruptions and arrests, a 38% increase, and more," Patel said. "We will continue to use every resource we have to detect and prevent acts of terrorism and wipe out their networks all over the country. Thank you to FBI Minneapolis, who did an outstanding job in the investigation and likely saved lives."
FBI Director Kash Patel conducts a news conference at the Department of Justice. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)
President Donald Trump also praised the FBI’s handling of the case while speaking to reporters Wednesday.
"I did hear about it. And they did a great job. The FBI did a great job," Trump said. The arrest capped an FBI investigation that began around December 2024 and eventually involved a confidential human source who communicated extensively with Mohamud over encrypted messaging and social media platforms, according to investigators.
Those conversations initially centered on Mohamud allegedly wanting to leave the United States and join al-Shabaab, the Somalia-based terrorist organization. In May, he allegedly told the source he was "so excited to make hijrah" and wanted to go to Somalia, get married and "fight the enemies of Allah." He said he planned to work for about six weeks to save $2,000 for a plane ticket, according to the affidavit.
By July, however, investigators say his plans had changed.
Mohamud allegedly told the source he did not have enough money to travel to Somalia and wrote, "so i will do attack here." He later discussed buying two pistols online and going to the Mall of America or the Minnesota State Fair around Christmas, according to the affidavit.
DENVER MAN'S ESCAPE EXPOSES CHILLING TREN DE ARAGUA KIDNAPPING PLOT THAT LANDS TRIO IN PRISON
Mohamud allegedly discussed attacking the Mall of America with an assault rifle and told the source he could "drive straight to the crowded place and start shooting." In September, investigators say he also sent the source a selfie-style video pledging allegiance to ISIS and its leader.
The FBI then arranged an undercover weapons transaction. On Sept. 25, the source told Mohamud a "brother" could sell him an AK-style rifle, magazines and ammunition, and Mohamud allegedly indicated he wanted the weapon to be fully automatic.
On Tuesday, Mohamud met the supposed ISIS-connected "brother" — actually an undercover FBI employee — and allegedly paid $800 for an AK-47-style rifle, four magazines and roughly 200 rounds of ammunition. The rifle had been rendered inoperable, though the ammunition was live. During the meeting, Mohamud allegedly said he planned to carry out a shooting at a "kuffar festival" at the Mall of America.

Mohamud left the vehicle with the rifle, magazines and ammunition in a duffel bag and was arrested at gunpoint by FBI agents, according to the affidavit.

articles.title_zh: Rare World War II aircraft on display in Huntsville
articles.content_orig:
HUNTSVILLE, Ala. ( WAFF ) - A rare piece of World War II history is in Huntsville today. The B-29 Superfortress known as Doc is at Huntsville’s airport as part of a tour stop this week.
Doc is one of only two B-29s still flying today. More than 1,600 were built in Wichita during the war.
It is joined by a P-51 Mustang. Those are rare too. Only about 150 of them are still around.
Visitors got a chance to see the aircraft up close and learn about the crews who designed, built and flew them.
“It’s a pretty special opportunity...really makes the history jump off the page,” Josh Wells said.
Wells said the event also helps younger generations understand an important piece of history.

articles.title_orig: Parliament calls for principled EU-China policy that combines dialogue, fair trade, and human rights
articles.title_zh: Parliament calls for principled EU-China policy that combines dialogue, fair trade, and human rights
articles.content_orig:
The European Parliament has advocated establishing a stronger, more principled EU-China policy that balances dialogue with the promotion of European interests. In a recommendation approved on Wednesday by a vote of 454 in favour, 86 against, and 110 abstentions, Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) highlighted the EU’s commitment to fostering a multilateral world. They underscored the importance of engaging with China on pressing global challenges, including peace and security, climate change, and human rights.
At the same time, MEPs acknowledged that bilateral relations have reached a critical juncture, largely due to China’s unfair economic practices and its position concerning Russia’s war against Ukraine. They expressed substantial concern over verified reports indicating that the Chinese military has trained Russian military personnel for involvement in Ukraine.
MEPs contend that the EU should work closely with the United States, G7 partners, and other like-minded nations to encourage China to use its influence over Russia to help end the conflict.
“Today’s majority marks a turning point in Europe’s China policy. With this week’s Franco-German initiative, a broad EU consensus is emerging on the need for a more balanced economic relationship with China. I hope Commissioner Šefčovič will take this united economic message to Beijing tomorrow. But this report goes even further: we want cooperation with China where possible, while standing firm on our security and values. As long as fundamental differences persist, systemic rivalry will also be part of our relationship,” rapporteur Hilde Vautmans (Renew, BE) said.
Direct engagement between the European Parliament and Chinese authorities resumed last year, after a suspension that began in 2021 when the Chinese government imposed sanctions on several MEPs in response to the EU’s human rights sanctions against certain Chinese officials and organisations. Between March and June 2026, three parliamentary delegations visited China, with a fourth visit scheduled for later in October 2026.
MEPs emphasised the urgent need to address the potential risks associated with the EU’s economic dependency on China. They called for a comprehensive de-risking strategy that focuses on critical raw materials, pharmaceuticals, batteries, electric vehicles, information and communication technology, semiconductors, and other strategic sectors. The Parliament has also called for enhanced investment screening and protection of vital technologies, infrastructure, and supply chains.
Furthermore, MEPs identified several challenges facing the EU economy, such as China’s industrial overcapacity, state subsidies, and barriers limiting European firms’ access to the Chinese market. They have called for reciprocity and a level playing field in trade and investment, supporting balanced EU actions when China does not adequately open its markets. They also advocated strengthening Global Gateway partnerships to provide a credible alternative to China’s Belt and Road Initiative, especially in Africa and Latin America.
The report reaffirms the EU’s One China policy and opposes any unilateral changes to the status quo in Taiwan through force or coercion. MEPs called for heightened resilience against cyber threats, foreign interference, espionage, and hybrid challenges, while also demanding a reinforced human rights dialogue with China focused on issues such as repression, forced labour, and policies in Tibet and Xinjiang.
The Parliament expressed significant concern about the recent adoption of the Law on Promoting Ethnic Unity and Progress and its potential to entrench assimilationist policies further. They also called for the unconditional release of political prisoners.

articles.title_orig: New Production of Lord of the Rings Musical to Embark on World Tour
articles.title_zh: New Production of Lord of the Rings Musical to Embark on World Tour
articles.content_orig:
This new production will be directed by Bruce Guthrie.
October 07, 2026 By Diep Tran
The road goes ever on, especially if you're a Lord of the Rings musical. A new stage production called The Lord of the Rings – The Epic Stage Adventure will world premiere at the Zorlu Performing Arts Center in Istanbul October 8, 2027. Further touring stops will include Bucharest, Prague, Warsaw, Thessaloniki, Tallinn, Athens, Sofia, Zagreb, and Dubai, with more (including venues in Europe) to be announced.
Based on J.R.R. Tolkien's fantasy novels, the new production will be directed by Bruce Guthrie, head of film and theatre at the National Centre for Performing Arts, Mumbai. It will feature scenic, video, and puppetry design by Tony and Olivier Award winner Andrzej Goulding ( Life of Pi ), and a score by Academy Award winner A.R. Rahman , the Finnish folk group Värttinä, and Tony Award Winner Christopher Nightingale, with book and lyrics by Shaun McKenna and Matthew Warchus .
It follows the hobbit Frodo as he embarks on a quest—alongside a fellowship composed of an elf, a dwarf, some men, and other hobbits—to destroy the One Ring and save Middle Earth.
The Lord of the Rings stage musical first premiered in 2006 at Princess of Wales Theatre in Toronto, before opening in the West End in 2007 at Theatre Royal, Drury Lane. A well-received production, which originated in 2023 at the Watermill Theatre in the U.K. just finished a North American and international tour. The forthcoming touring production features a new creative team.
Lord of the Rings is is produced by Kevin Wallace and William Bennett for KW Productions, George Isaak for People Entertainment Group, and Middle-earth Enterprises, LLC, with Peter Huntley and Callum Runciman as executive producers and general managers for Smart Entertainment.
Tickets for the Istanbul engagement will be available at Zorlupsm.com .
Visit LOTRmusical.com for more information.

articles.title_orig: Rubio calls for "unapologetic pursuit of national power," invoking ancient Greece in Acropolis speech
articles.title_zh: Rubio calls for "unapologetic pursuit of national power," invoking ancient Greece in Acropolis speech
articles.content_orig:
Athens — As the United States wages a costly war with Iran and Europe struggles with the grinding conflict in Ukraine, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stood before the Acropolis on Wednesday and reached back more than two millennia to argue that the answer to the West's current problems can be found, at least in part, in ancient Greece.
In a speech timed to the sunset from the Pnyx, where Athenians gathered for their democratic assembly, Rubio cast ancient Greece as the source not only of Western democracy and philosophy, but of what he described as the character that fueled the West's rise.
"Here, in Athens, we found the first full realization of all the essential traits that would come to define the West," Rubio said, citing "fierce individuality and relentless ambition," and "a yearning for discovery, for adventure, risk and glory."
He argued that those modern Western societies had allowed those qualities to erode.
"The ideal of many ideologies in our time has, frankly, become a world of perfect safety, a world devoid of risk or failure, where neither the glory of victory, nor the shame of defeat," Rubio said. "We hold the most exceptional things among us hostage to the average, the ordinary, the mediocre."
His remarks were delivered before roughly 250 invited guests, including senior Greek government officials, members of the diplomatic corps and representatives of the business, educational and cultural sectors, according to a senior State Department official.
The speech expanded on themes Rubio laid out at the Munich Security Conference in February, when he warned that Europe faced "civilizational erasure" and argued that the U.S. and Europe needed to recover a shared Western identity. Still, his conciliatory tone in Munich came as a relief to European officials after Vice President JD Vance had used the same stage a year earlier to sharply rebuke the continent's leaders.
In front of the Acropolis, Rubio traced the development of the West from ancient Greece through Rome, European Christianity and eventually the United States, citing Alexander the Great, Caesar, Charlemagne and Columbus along the way. He portrayed America's frontier expansion, industrial development and space program as later expressions of the same drive.
Rubio said the West now stands at a crossroads, "because the next decade and the decisions we make will write the story of the next century."
"The course we take will determine whether the West maintains its place at the head of the world or resigns itself to a future of atrophy and servitude and decline. We will either choose to act now or lose the choice to act at all," he said.
"Under President Trump, the United States has made its choice," Rubio continued. "We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power, to take back control of our critical supply chains, to reindustrialize our economy, to rebuild our defense, to fight for dominance of the technologies and industries of the future."
The history Rubio presented was arguably selective. He spoke relatively little about democracy or political equality at a site closely associated with both, focusing instead on competition, national loyalty and the willingness to take risks. He argued that modern societies too often seek "perfect safety" and concern themselves more with "the comfort of the worst than the potential of the best."
"The men who made the Parthenon, they built upwards. They held that the highest and most noble aspiration in life was to surpass all others, to strive to be the best in all things," he said.
The highly produced speech came during a trip largely devoted to more immediate questions of American power: where U.S. forces can operate, how NATO allies can help counter Russia and Iran, and how American energy can displace Russian supplies in Europe.
Greece was the second stop on a three-country tour that began in Iceland and ends in Portugal on Thursday. In Iceland, amid growing U.S. attention to Arctic security, Rubio left open the possibility of an increased American military presence, saying, "We'd never do anything without cooperating with officials here about what's available. I think there is a willingness to do more together."
In Athens, Rubio met Greek Foreign Minister George Gerapetritis for the sixth U.S.-Greece Strategic Dialogue, focused on defense, energy and regional security. At a news conference Wednesday, Rubio called Greece a "strong and model NATO ally," while Gerapetritis said Greece could provide maritime assistance in the Strait of Hormuz if a viable peace process is established.
Rubio was also asked by CBS News whether he was confident U.S. Ambassador Kimberly Guilfoyle's tenure had complied with State Department ethics rules, amid congressional scrutiny over allegations that Guilfoyle used her diplomatic position to benefit private business interests in Greece.
"This is not the format where we're going to address this," Rubio said. "Suffice it to say our embassy has been doing a great job. Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador." Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.
Rubio's visit and Acropolis address come at a complex moment for the Trump administration.
The U.S. is seven months into its war with Iran and has yet to secure an agreement to end it. Vice President JD Vance said this week that Iran would need to make a "meaningful" reduction in its uranium enrichment capacity, raising questions about whether the administration was backing away from its earlier insistence on zero enrichment.
Asked Wednesday by CBS News to clarify the U.S. position, Rubio declined to say what level of enrichment, if any, Washington might accept.
"I don't understand what the confusion is about the nuclear program. Iran cannot have a nuclear weapon. Simple, period and end of story," he said. "I'm not going to go into, you know, into the details about what would be acceptable or not."
The war has also helped push oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, adding an economic and political cost at home as the midterm elections approach.
In his remarks before the Acropolis, Rubio directly raised Iran. After invoking the Spartans at Thermopylae and Achilles' pursuit of glory at Troy, he contrasted Western ideas of sacrifice with what he called a "cult of death" among Iran's "radical mullahs."
"Our heroes may be willing to die for their cause, but they do not worship death," he said.
The speech also comes as Rubio's own political future attracts increasing attention. President Trump has publicly raised both Rubio and Vice President Vance as possible future standard-bearers for his movement.
Rubio did not overtly mention his own ambitions Wednesday, but pointed to recent administration achievements, including the Greenland deal he helped broker last month.
"It is a vision we saw in action," Rubio said, arguing the agreement would "reshape the Arctic and bolster the security of all of NATO."
"We want to win together," he said. "We must win together."

articles.title_orig: Nuclear clocks finally see the light
articles.title_zh: Nuclear clocks finally see the light
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for registering with Physics World If you'd like to change your details at any time, please visit My account
Two independent teams have realized the first clocks based on transitions within atomic nuclei. The new nuclear clocks represent the culmination of more than 20 years of research and could become vital tools in precision tests of fundamental physics.
Today’s most accurate clocks “tick” whenever an electron transitions between two specific hyperfine levels in the ground state of an atom. These atomic clocks form a vital part of technologies such as satellite navigation and telecommunications networks. They also contribute to fundamental research in dark matter searches and gravitational wave detection.
Traditionally, the hyperfine levels used in atomic clocks are separated by gaps with frequencies in the microwave range. However, more modern atomic clocks use higher-frequency optical transitions. Known as optical clocks, they are more precise because they “tick” more often within a given period, enabling finer measurements of time passing.
Clocks based on atomic nuclei could, in principle, be more precise still. First proposed in the late 1990s, they are less prone to disturbances from electromagnetic fields, and they exploit transitions at even higher (ultraviolet) frequencies. Getting such clocks to work, however, proved no easy feat, because driving these narrow nuclear transitions requires highly stable lasers with extremely small bandwidths.
Two independent teams are now reporting a breakthrough in this field. Writing in Nature , they describe realizing working nuclear clocks based on transitions in nuclei of thorium-229.
Members of the first team, which is led by Ekkehard Peik at the Physikalisch-Technische Bundesanstalt (PTB) in Germany and Thorsten Schumm from TU Wien in Austria and includes colleagues in Germany, Austria and Czechia, had previously made several key advances. Peik and Schumm’s group were the first to demonstrate laser excitation of the thorium-229 nuclear transition . They were also the first to embed thorium-229 within crystals of calcium fluoride (CaF 2 ), creating a solid-state device which, unlike (optical) atomic clocks, does not use trapped atoms or ions.
The second team, led by Shiqian Ding from Tsinghua University and including collaborators at 13 other institutions across China, has likewise chalked up notable achievements, including a demonstration of the first continuous-wave narrow-linewidth UV laser at the crucial wavelength of 148.4 nm. Because China has limited access to thorium-229, Ding and colleagues also developed an approach for growing small single crystals that requires only 1.4 μ g of the isotope.
In the latest work, both teams used thorium-229 embedded in millimetre-sized CaF 2 crystals and driven by narrow-linewidth, continuous-wave UV lasers, although the nonlinear processes used to generate the laser light were different. They also both used direct absorption spectroscopy through the crystal to monitor how well they were exciting the nuclear resonance, plus a feedback loop to lock the laser frequency onto the desired transition. They thus created stabilized nuclear clocks that they could compare continuously to frequency standards derived from atomic clocks.
At this point, the teams’ efforts diverged. Whereas Schumm and colleagues were able to embed more thorium-229 into their CaF 2 crystals, Ding and colleagues generated laser light at higher powers. Both features tend to produce more stable clocks with a higher signal-to-noise ratio, although the fractional frequency instability in the Tsinghua device was lower, at 5 x 10 -13 /√τ/s (where τ is the averaging time), compared to 3 x 10 -12 /√τ/s in the PTB-TU Wien collaboration.
The PTB-TU Wien team applied their nuclear clock to fundamental physics, using it to search for ultralight scalar dark matter couplings and constrain fluctuations/drifts in the nuclear transition energy. Their results set limits on how dark matter can couple to photons and the strong nuclear force that are comparable to those derived from today’s best atomic clocks.
The primary focus of Ding and colleagues’ work was on technical aspects such as high-power vacuum ultraviolet (VUV) interrogation, clock performance, inter-crystal reproducibility and metrological consistency. The clock transition frequencies they measured in two independently fabricated crystals agreed both with each other and with previous measurements of the thorium-229 transition made using VUV frequency combs at JILA in the US.
Peik says that he and his team are now working on boosting their laser power, improving the signal-to-noise ratio in their detectors, and studying the structure of the thorium dopant in their crystal to understand what determines the linewidth of the nuclear resonance within it. “We have now seen 30 kHz linewidth, but the natural linewidth should be way below 1 Hz, which would enable more stable clock operation,” he tells Physics World .
Nuclear clock ticks ever closer
Ding says that an important next step for his team is to develop better host crystals than CaF 2 , which could lead to a substantially narrower nuclear transition and improve both stability and accuracy. He is also interested in creating a trapped-ion thorium nuclear clock that would be more isolated from its environment and could re-use many of the quantum control techniques developed for atomic and ion clocks. “It is technically much more difficult, but I think this route may ultimately provide the highest accuracy,” he says.
Victor Flambaum , a theorist from the University of New South Wales, Australia who was not involved in either project, calls the teams’ devices the “first prototypes of nuclear clocks”. He is excited by their potential for uncovering new physics effects, such as those produced by dark matter, which are expected to be very small. “We have shown that in nuclear clocks these effects are strongly enhanced,” he says.
